Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program and complemented by ten distinct provincial and territorial tax credit regimes—is undergoing its most substantial statutory transformation in over a decade.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, federal legislative amendments introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, expanded in Budget 2025, and enacted via Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) have fundamentally restructured the federal SR&ED program. Specifically, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in refundable credits annually), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored both the income tax deduction and ITC eligibility for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional pre-claim approval process delivering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, while the Province of Québec enacted its landmark Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating seven legacy R&D tax measures into a unified 30% / 20% refundable credit covering both R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
1. Executive Summary and the 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul
1.1 Dual-Incentive Mechanics of the Federal SR&ED Program

The federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is the single largest federal support program for business R&D in Canada, with 24,160 claims filed and $4.6 billion in investment tax credits allowed by the CRA in its 2025–2026 fiscal year (April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026). Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (which executes technical and financial administration), the program operates through two distinct yet interconnected statutory mechanisms under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA).

First, under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in the taxation year into the Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool. The taxpayer may deduct any portion of this net pool in computing business income for the current taxation year—overriding the general capital expenditure prohibition in section 18—or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years.

Second, under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their net "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Depending on the taxpayer's legal classification, size, and expenditure type, unused ITCs remaining after offsetting Part I federal income tax payable may be refunded in cash (at rates of 100% or 40% under section 127.1) or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years.
1.2 Chronology and Enactment of the 2024–2026 Reforms (Bill C-15)

Following national stakeholder consultations launched in Budget 2024 to modernize Canada's innovation incentives, the federal government rolled out a comprehensive statutory reform package in two stages before enshrining the measures into law in March 2026.

In the first stage, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) proposed a six-year, $1.9 billion reform package effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. That initial announcement proposed increasing the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million (up to $1.575 million in refundable credits), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), allowing Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect a revenue-based phase-out formula, and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays made on or after December 16, 2024.

In the second stage, Budget 2025 confirmed the implementation of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement reforms and proposed to further increase the annual expenditure limit on which the enhanced 35% ITC can be earned from the previously announced $4.5 million to $6.0 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. In Table 1 (Revenue Impacts of Proposed Tax Measures) of the Budget 2025 Tax Measures: Supplementary Information, the Department of Finance projected the incremental fiscal cost of this expansion at $3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030, totalling $293 million over five years (in addition to the $1.9 billion baseline reform package).

In the third stage, on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent, formally enacting the amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. Between May and October 2026, the CRA published updated versions of Form T661 (May 15, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (May 22, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026, and updated further in October 2026), the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), and the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026).

body.text: 2. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (activités de recherche scientifique et de développement expérimental) codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Unlike general accounting or commercial conceptions of product development, subsection 248(1) establishes a rigorous, closed-end legal definition structured into three core pillars of eligible work (paragraphs (a) to (c)), an enumerated list of eight directly supporting activities (paragraph (d)), and seven categorical statutory exclusions (paragraphs (e) to (k)).

Under the opening preamble of subsection 248(1), SR&ED means "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of the following categories:

Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research (Recherche pure): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research is typically conducted in laboratory or academic settings to uncover fundamental scientific principles or phenomena—for example, studying the characteristics of a newly discovered virus to better understand its properties—and its results are usually published in scientific journals.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research (Recherche appliquée): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research builds upon scientific inquiry but directs the investigation toward a defined practical objective—such as efforts to develop a vaccine against a new virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that newly discovered virus.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development (Développement expérimental): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that a taxpayer does not need to invent an entirely brand-new product or disruptive technology; resolving underlying technological uncertainties to achieve incremental advances in an existing manufacturing process, software architecture, or material composition fully qualifies.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Eligible Support Work: In applying the definition in respect of a taxpayer, SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive categories: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work never qualifies as SR&ED on its own, with a narrow statutory exception under subsection 37(13) for non-arm's length contractors performing support work for a related party conducting core SR&ED.
Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k)

Even where a project involves genuine basic research, applied research, or experimental development, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to seven enumerated activities (collectively termed "the exclusions"):

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e) — Market Research or Sales Promotion: Includes examining consumer buying habits, use of leisure time, consumer needs or wants, attitudes toward existing or test-marketed products, market development, market verification, general market identification, market demonstration, developing customer acceptance, and studying market requirements.
Paragraph 248(1)(f) — Quality Control or Routine Testing: Encompasses quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.

Paragraph 248(1)(g) — Social Sciences or Humanities: Excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities (note that management is also classified as a social science and is excluded under paragraph (g); however, psychological research is specifically carved out as eligible support work under paragraph (d) under qualifying circumstances).

Paragraph 248(1)(h) — Mineral, Petroleum, or Natural Gas Exploration and Production: Excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (whereas concurrent SR&ED work to develop new extraction processes or equipment remains eligible while actual prospecting/drilling is excluded).

Paragraph 248(1)(i) — Commercial Production or Commercial Use: Excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j) — Style Changes: Excludes aesthetic, cosmetic, or fashion modifications that do not seek to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty.
Paragraph 248(1)(k) — Routine Data Collection: Excludes gathering data for standard business or operational purposes rather than directly supporting SR&ED.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives emphasize, the key feature that distinguishes eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "testing" or "data collection") from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing scientific research or experimental development, it qualifies under paragraph (d); if it is carried out for some other commercial or operational reason, it is excluded.
2.2 The CRA's "Why and How" Framework vs. The Five Questions

In August 2021, the CRA consolidated its administrative guidance into the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (replacing the 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy). The updated guidelines frame subsection 248(1) around two core statutory requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—while confirming that both the two requirements and the traditional five questions derive from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1).

The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement) requires that the work be conducted for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement—defined as the generation of information or discovery of knowledge that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technology. A scientific or technological advancement cannot be achieved unless there is an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty, which is a limitation in the current state of scientific knowledge or technology that occurs when existing design methods are inapplicable, requirements do not conform to existing standards, there are too many variables or unknowns, or parameters lie outside the normal operating range. Acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search) mandates that the work be carried out through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This requires: (a) observing and analysing the problem against available knowledge and experience; (b) generating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation (formulating a hypothesis); (c) testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis; (d) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis (where the idea can evolve and change as a result of testing); and (e) keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses.
2.3 Section 37 of the Income Tax Act: The Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act governs the calculation, deduction, and carryforward of the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool. Unlike ordinary business expenses deducted under section 9, section 37 operates as a cumulative, non-expiring tax pool.
Additions to the Section 37 Pool (Paragraphs 37(1)(a) to (c.3))
Under subsection 37(1), where a taxpayer carries on a business in Canada in a taxation year, the taxpayer may add the following eligible expenditures to their deductible SR&ED expenditure pool:

items: Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) — In-House Current Expenditures: Expenditures of a current nature made in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer.

Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) — Contracted Current Expenditures: Expenditures of a current nature made in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer (subcontracted SR&ED), and related to a business of the taxpayer.

Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) — Third-Party Payments to Canadian Corporations ("A Entities"): Payments to a corporation resident in Canada to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED.

Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) — Third-Party Payments to Approved Entities ("B to E Entities"): Payments to (A) an approved association that undertakes SR&ED, (B) an approved university, college, research institute, or other similar institution, (C) a corporation resident in Canada and exempt from Part I tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) (a non-profit SR&ED corporation), or (E) an approved organization that makes payments to an association, institution, or corporation described in clauses (A) to (C) (note: clause (D) was repealed in 1996), to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results.

Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii) — Corporate Payments to Non-Profit R&D Corporations: Payments by a corporate taxpayer to a corporation exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j) for basic or applied research carried on in Canada whose primary purpose is for use in conjunction with other current or future SR&ED of the taxpayer and that has technological potential for application to other unrelated businesses.

Paragraph 37(1)(b) — Capital Expenditures (Restored After December 15, 2024): Expenditures of a capital nature made by the taxpayer (after December 15, 2024) on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, related to a business of the taxpayer, in respect of property acquired that would otherwise be depreciable property of the taxpayer (other than land or a leasehold interest in land, and subject to paragraph 37(8)(d)/(e) exclusions for buildings and leasehold interests in buildings other than a prescribed special-purpose building). Any deduction claimed under subsection 37(1) in respect of capital property is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA).

Paragraphs 37(1)(c), (c.1), (c.2), and (c.3) — Repayments and Recapture Adjustments: Paragraph (c) adds repayments in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(d). Paragraph (c.1) adds amounts included in the taxpayer's income under paragraph 12(1)(v) for previous taxation years. Paragraph (c.2) adds amounts added to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable under subsections 127(27), 127(29), or 127(34) for preceding taxation years due to SR&ED ITC recapture. Paragraph (c.3) adds partnership ITC recapture excess amounts referred to in subsection 127(30).

body.text: Geographic Scope and Foreign SR&ED Rules (Subsections 37(1.1), 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2))

Under paragraph 37(1.1)(b), expenditures made for the prosecution of SR&ED in the exclusive economic zone of Canada (within the meaning of the Oceans Act), or in the airspace above or seabed/subsoil below that zone, are eligible on the same footing as mainland Canadian SR&ED.

While SR&ED performed outside Canada generally does not enter the subsection 37(1) pool or earn an ITC, subsection 37(1.4) deems an expenditure determined under subsection 37(1.5) for salary or wages paid to an employee performing SR&ED outside Canada to be made in Canada. Under subsection 37(1.5), this permissible foreign wage amount is the lesser of:

items: Paragraph 37(1.5)(a): Total expenditures made in the taxation year (after February 25, 2008) for salary or wages paid to the taxpayer's employees who were resident in Canada at the time the expense was incurred, for SR&ED carried on outside Canada that was (i) directly undertaken by the taxpayer, (ii) related to a business of the taxpayer, and (iii) solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer—provided under paragraph 37(9)(b) that the taxpayer reasonably believes the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by a foreign country because of the employee's presence or activity in that country; and

Paragraph 37(1.5)(b): 10% of the total expenditures made in the taxation year for salary or wages paid to employees in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by the taxpayer and related to their business.

body.text: Under subsection 37(2) (Research Outside Canada), any current SR&ED expenditures incurred outside Canada that do not fall within the 10% Canadian-resident employee rule in subsections 37(1.4)–(1.5)—such as foreign subcontractor payments or payments to approved foreign universities or research institutes where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results—may be deducted directly in computing current-year business income. However, subsection 37(2) expenditures cannot be added to the subsection 37(1) carryforward pool, cannot be reported on Form T661, and earn 0% ITC.
Reductions to the Section 37 Pool (Paragraphs 37(1)(d) to (h))

Under paragraphs 37(1)(d) through (h), the total pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced by: (1) all government assistance and non-government assistance (such as provincial R&D tax credits and grants) in respect of SR&ED that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(d)); (2) provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); (3) federal SR&ED ITCs deducted (or deemed deducted via cash refund) under subsection 127(5) in preceding taxation years attributable to prescribed proxy amounts, current qualified expenditures, or SR&ED qualified expenditure pools (paragraph 37(1)(e)); (4) amounts previously deducted under subsection 37(1) in computing business income in preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(f)); (5) amounts deducted under section 61.3 in preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(f.1)); (6) twice the amount claimed under subparagraph 194(2)(a)(ii) (paragraph 37(1)(g)); and (7) loss restriction event reductions determined under subsection 37(6.1) following an acquisition of control of a corporation (paragraph 37(1)(h)).
Statutory Restrictions in Subsections 37(4) through 37(13)

Under subsection 37(4), no deduction may be made under section 37 in respect of an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. Under subsection 37(5), no deduction is allowed under section 37 for an expenditure in respect of which a charitable deduction or tax credit is claimed under section 110.1 or section 118.1 of the Act. Under paragraph 37(8)(c), a claimant deriving all or substantially all (90% or more) of its revenue from the prosecution of SR&ED is considered to satisfy the requirement that its SR&ED expenditures relate to a business carried on by the claimant.

Finally, under subsection 37(11), a taxpayer claiming a deduction under section 37 must file a prescribed form (Form T661) on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year, containing (a) prescribed information in respect of the expenditure and (b) claim preparer information as defined in subsection 162(5.3). Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), if the taxpayer fails to file the prescribed form containing the prescribed information in accordance with subsection 37(11), no amount in respect of the expenditure may be deducted under subsection 37(1) and the expenditure is deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED for the purposes of the Act.
3. Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers (Sections 127 and 127.1 ITA)
3.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is governed by subsections 127(5) through 127(36) of the Income Tax Act, with refundability governed by section 127.1. At the end of each taxation year, a claimant calculates its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" (defined in subsection 127(9)), which does not carry over from year to year but serves as the annual base on which the current-year ITC is generated.

The Basic ITC Rate (15%): Under subsection 127(9), the basic ITC rate is 15% of the excess of the claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year over any provincial super-allowance benefit amount. (The basic rate was reduced from 20% to 15% for taxation years ending after 2013). The 15% basic rate applies to: (1) corporations other than qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs; (2) CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their annual expenditure limit; (3) sole proprietorships (individuals); (4) partners of a partnership; and (5) beneficiaries of trusts.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35% — 15% Basic + 20% Subsection 127(10.1) Addition): Under subsection 127(10.1), qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an additional 20% ITC on the lesser of their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool and their annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, resulting in a combined enhanced ITC rate of 35%.
3.2 Qualifying Corporate Entities: CCPCs and ECPCs
To access the 35% enhanced ITC rate, a corporation must satisfy the statutory definition of either a CCPC or an ECPC:

Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC — Subsection 125(7) ITA): A corporation that, at the end of the taxation year, is a private corporation, is resident in Canada (and was either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada from June 18, 1971 to the end of the taxation year), has no class of shares of its capital stock listed on a designated stock exchange, and is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation defined in Regulation 6700), by a Canadian-resident corporation that lists its shares on a designated stock exchange outside Canada, or by any combination thereof. Furthermore, if all of its shares owned by a non-resident person, by a public corporation (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange were owned by one single person, that person must not own sufficient shares to control the corporation.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC — Subsection 127(9) ITA): Enacted by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (as announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), ECPCs can earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate and claim refundable ITCs up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, subject to consolidated group aggregation rules where the ECPC is a member of a consolidated group.
3.3 The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum annual expenditure limit on which a CCPC or ECPC (and its associated corporations or consolidated group members) can earn the 35% enhanced ITC has doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
A. Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit decreased based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) for the previous taxation year: once prior-year taxable capital reached $10,000,000, the expenditure limit began to decrease linearly and became nil when prior-year taxable capital reached $50,000,000:

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 and Budget 2025 increased the base expenditure limit to $6,000,000 and expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds so that the gradual reduction begins at $15,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada and the expenditure limit becomes nil at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out range across all CCPCs in an associated group):

Similarly, the qualifying income limit for CCPCs—which determines whether a CCPC's prior-year taxable income is below the threshold required to be a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 40% refundability on basic 15% ITCs—is scaled by prior-year taxable capital using the formula $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000] for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 (where A is prior-year taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000 up to $40,000,000), and $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000] for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (where A is prior-year taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000 up to $60,000,000).
B. Average Annual Revenue Phase-Out Method (ECPCs and Electing CCPCs)

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the reduction of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is calculated using the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation that is a member of the group for the taxation year in question over the preceding 3 fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that 3-year period. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs may elect (by submitting the prescribed form under subsection 127(10.32)) to use this same 3-year average annual revenue method for calculating the expenditure limit instead of the taxable capital method.
C. Associated Corporations, Short Taxation Years, and Multiple Year-Ends

Associated CCPCs must allocate the expenditure limit among group members using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Under subsection 127(10.5), if a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), its expenditure limit is prorated by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365. For example, if Corporation P is allocated $3,000,000 of the group's expenditure limit and has a short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31, 2027, its expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,328. Specific rules also apply when a CCPC or ECPC has more than 1 taxation year ending in a calendar year and is associated (or in a consolidated group) in 2 or more of those taxation years with another CCPC or ECPC having a taxation year ending in that same calendar year.
3.4 Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1 ITA)

When a claimant's SR&ED ITC earned in the taxation year exceeds its federal Part I tax otherwise payable, section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act determines the percentage of the unclaimed ITC balance that is refunded in cash. Any SR&ED ITC refunded in the taxation year is deemed to be an ITC applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby reducing the ITCs available for carryforward or carryback. body.text: 3.5 Carryback, Carryforward, Exempt Income, and Partnership Rules

3-Year Carryback and 20-Year Carryforward: Under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9), any unused current-year ITC (the portion not deducted against Part I tax or refunded in the current year) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years and carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable. The carryback to a prior taxation year is limited to the lesser of: (1) the portion of current-year ITCs not deductible against Part I tax in the current year; and (2) the Part I tax otherwise payable in the previous year in excess of ITCs already available in that previous year.

Acquisition of Control Restrictions: If control of a corporation is acquired, statutory restrictions limit carrying forward ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and carrying back ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.

Exempt Income Disqualification: No amount shall be considered a claimant's ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax.

Partnership Allocation Rules (Subsections 96(1), 127(8), and 127(28)–(31)): In computing the income of a partnership, SR&ED expenditures are accounted for at the partnership level, and the ITC is calculated at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate and then allocated under subsection 127(8) to eligible partners (individuals, corporations, or trusts) at the end of the partnership's fiscal period. A partner's allocation is capped by the taxpayer's at-risk amount in respect of the partnership at the end of that fiscal period (less any amounts required by a clean economy allocation provision under subsection 127.47(1) to be added in computing a clean economy tax credit). Furthermore, the ITC allocated to a member of a partnership that is a corporation (other than a qualifying corporation) cannot be refunded.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Methodologies
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election

When preparing Form T661, a claimant must select on lines 160 and 162 of Part 3, Section A whether to calculate its SR&ED expenditures for the taxation year using the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act and Regulation 2900(4)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the Act and Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3)).

body.text: 4.2 Salary or Wages and Specified Employee Limitations

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment, including fees for services not rendered in the course of business, taxable benefits under section 6 of the Act, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, bonuses, tips, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, and commissions, but excluding superannuation, pension benefits, and retiring allowances. Under the Proxy Method, eligible salary or wages are restricted to employees directly engaged in SR&ED (based on actual hands-on tasks performed, including non-specialized employees operating machinery or feeding raw materials for an experiment under qualified supervision, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects, and first-line technical supervision directing the course of ongoing SR&ED, while excluding clerical/administrative staff and non-technological management functions). Where an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their employment time directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be for SR&ED.
Included and Excluded Wage Components

Allowable salary or wage amounts include base salary or wages, cash outlays for taxable benefits, non-cash taxable benefits (provided the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, does not include GST/HST or PST for which an input tax credit can be claimed, and the actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense), inducement payments, non-competition payments, and—solely for employees other than specified employees—bonuses and remuneration based on profits.
Conversely, five categories of employee-related outlays are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages:

items: Employer's Share of Related Benefits: Employer contributions to CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved pension plans, superannuation plan premiums, medical/dental/optical insurance plans, supplementary sick benefits, and employee savings plans are excluded from salary or wages (under the Traditional Method, related benefits may qualify on line 360 as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures).
Stock Option Benefits (Section 7 ITA): Stock option benefits (options granted or shares issued) are excluded because they are considered not to be an expenditure incurred by the claimant.
Extended Vacation or Sick Leave: Leave in excess of normal annual leave earned is excluded because the employee is not performing duties during that period.

Retiring Allowances: Excluded from salary or wages by definition under subsection 248(1), though under the Traditional Method a portion of a retiring allowance may be claimed as an overhead expenditure under Regulation 2900(2)(c) if it satisfies the incremental test and is reasonably allocated using total career salary, career SR&ED salary allowed, and years employed.

Unpaid Salary or Wages — The 180-Day Rule (Subsection 78(4) ITA): Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, employee remuneration that remains unpaid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year and is excluded from the SR&ED pool for that year (when subsequently paid in a later year, it is deemed incurred in the year paid, but remains permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)(b)).

body.text: Rules and Caps for "Specified Employees"

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a "specified employee" of a person means an employee who is a specified shareholder of the person—defined as a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any other corporation that is related to the corporation (counting shares owned by persons with whom the taxpayer does not deal at arm's length)—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (under section 251). Four strict statutory restrictions govern specified employees:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Paragraph 37(9)(a) ITA): For both the Traditional and Proxy methods, an expenditure of a taxpayer does not include remuneration based on profits or a bonus where the remuneration or bonus is in respect of a specified employee of the taxpayer.

Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap — 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1) ITA): Under subsection 37(9.1), expenditures incurred by a taxpayer in a taxation year do not include expenses incurred in respect of salary or wages of a specified employee to the extent that those expenses exceed the formula A × (B ÷ 365), where A is 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year on which the employee is a specified employee of the taxpayer.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7)): In determining the PPA under the Proxy Method (Part 5 of Form T661, lines 852–858), the portion of salary or wages of a specified employee included in the salary base shall not exceed the lesser of:

Paragraph 2900(7)(a): 75% of the amount incurred by the taxpayer in the year in respect of total salary or wages of the specified employee (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, section 6/7 taxable benefits, and prior years' unpaid salary/wages paid in the year); and

Paragraph 2900(7)(b): The amount determined by the formula 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year in which the employee is employed by the taxpayer (with no proration for any portion of the year the employee was not a specified employee).

Associated Corporation Allocation Rules (Subsections 37(9.2)–(9.5) and Regulations 2900(8) & 2900(10)): Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the associated corporations must allocate the 5 × YMPE limit among themselves by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) in prescribed form accompanied by corporate resolutions. Similarly, under Regulations 2900(8) and 2900(10), the combined salary base inclusion across associated corporations (treating related individuals and partnerships with related/associated members as associated corporations) cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE.

body.text: 4.3 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Mechanics and Overall Cap (Regulation 2900(4)–(9))

For claimants electing the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 (line 820) as 55% of the claimant's eligible salary base (Regulation 2900(4)). Under Regulation 2900(9), regardless of whether an employee is a specified employee or a regular employee, four categories of remuneration must be excluded when calculating the salary base: (1) amounts described in section 6 (taxable benefits) or section 7 (employee stock options) of the Act; (2) amounts deemed under subsection 78(4) of the Act to have been incurred (unpaid remuneration from a prior year paid in the current taxation year, reported on line 310/315 of Form T661); (3) bonuses; and (4) remuneration based on profits.
The Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the taxation year, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA. The PPA for a taxation year in respect of a business shall not exceed the amount determined by the formula:
Overall Cap on PPA = A − B − C

where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the total of all amounts deducted in computing business income for the year under any of sections 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditures), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts) of the Act; and C is any amount incurred by the taxpayer in the year in respect of any outlay or expense made or incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building other than a special-purpose building. As noted in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the Overall Cap generally will not restrict the PPA if the claimant deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding the specified statutory deductions in B and building rent in C) for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
4.4 Traditional Method Overhead and Section 2902 Prescribed Expenditures

Claimants electing the Traditional Method do not calculate a PPA; instead, under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3), they claim actual current overhead and other expenditures on line 360 of Form T661.

Under Regulation 2900(2)(c), other current expenditures (or portions thereof) are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada if they satisfy two cumulative tests: (1) the "Directly Related" Test, which requires a direct linkage—without an intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED; and (2) the "Incremental" Test, which requires that the expenditure would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed monthly telephone or internet service charges are ordinary business expenses that fail the incremental test, whereas identifiable long-distance charges, incremental utilities, domestic travel and lodging to conduct testing at a customer location in Canada, SR&ED training costs in Canada, and waste disposal of scrap produced during active SR&ED (excluding waste disposal incurred after the SR&ED activity has finished) qualify.

Under Regulation 2900(3), expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada include: (a) the cost of maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment (which under paragraph 2900(3)(a) does not require separate directly related and incremental tests, though a fixed-cost maintenance contract generally will not meet the incremental test for overhead); and (b) other expenditures (or portions thereof) that are directly related to that provision and that would not have been incurred if those premises, facilities, or equipment had not existed.

Even under the Traditional Method, Regulation 2902 designates specific items as "prescribed expenditures" that are excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) and cannot earn an ITC:

items: Administrative salary or wages and related benefits in respect of a person whose duties are not all or substantially all (≥90%) directed to the prosecution of SR&ED, except to the extent described in Regulation 2900(2) or (3) (clause 2902(a)(i)(A));
A legal or accounting fee (clause 2902(a)(i)(B));
Interest and financing expenses described in any of paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the Act (clause 2902(a)(i)(C));
An entertainment expense (clause 2902(a)(i)(D));
An advertising or selling expense (clause 2902(a)(i)(E));
A conference or convention expense, even where attending a technical convention specific to the SR&ED project (clause 2902(a)(i)(F));
A due or fee in respect of membership in a scientific or technical society or organization (clause 2902(a)(i)(G)); and
A fine or penalty (clause 2902(a)(i)(H)).

body.text: 4.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

The "Body of a Thing" Test: Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, the term "materials for SR&ED" refers to all raw materials, substances, or other physical and tangible items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a thing (a tangible object) on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED being carried out. Items that do not compose the body of the object—such as broken or used laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas, or water used to generate steam for heat/energy), CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED (though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method). Conversely, seed, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides applied to experimental test plots, or metal parts and chemicals subjected to experimental galvanization or treatment, compose the body of the thing and qualify as materials for SR&ED.

Timing Rule: The cost of materials for SR&ED can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (and cannot be claimed in the year it is received from a supplier or removed from inventory for future SR&ED use), and must be paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year to earn an ITC.

Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed: "Materials consumed" are materials that are absorbed, used up, or broken down into small pieces—meaning they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless (scrap or resale value of less than 10% of original cost) as a result of the SR&ED. If 90% or more of the cost of a material is consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED, the entire cost is allowable as materials consumed. When materials for SR&ED have not been rendered virtually valueless after the SR&ED (or are recycled SR&ED materials or incorporated into an experimental production run, pilot plant, or custom asset), they constitute "materials transformed". While materials transformed are 100% allowable in the year transformed (strictly for the components involving SR&ED—costs of commercial portions of a custom product where no SR&ED occurred are not allowable), materials transformed are subject to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27)–(36) if the resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years.

4.7 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

After being repealed between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and equipment lease costs for property acquired (and available for use) or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ASA ≥90% Test — Paragraph 37(1)(b) & Regulation 2902(b))

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on line 390 and Part 6B Box 782 of Form T661, with the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties listed on line 262), the expenditure must be made after December 15, 2024 to acquire depreciable property (owned by the claimant or in which the claimant has a leasehold interest) that is available for use and meets one of two "All or Substantially All" (ASA, 90% or more) intention criteria at the time of acquisition:

items: It is intended to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or
All or substantially all (90% or more) of its value is intended to be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

body.text: While both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test can be claimed in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (as deemed CCA, and therefore must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8), under Regulation 2902(b)(iii) used property (property that has been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatever before it was acquired by the taxpayer, unless significantly refurbished to be considered new) is a prescribed expenditure excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures. Non-depreciable property (such as land or inventory) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (other than a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903) are excluded. The capital cost of the property includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs (excluding borrowing costs).
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9) & Regulation 2900(11))

When a claimant acquires new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (reported on line 504 and Part 6C Box 792 of Form T661) if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% up to less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada:

items: First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): Evaluated over the "first period," which starts when the property is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that acquisition date. If actual SR&ED usage exceeds 50% of operating time in the first period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost is deemed to be a qualified SR&ED expenditure for ITC purposes.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): Evaluated over the "second period," which starts when the property is acquired and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that acquisition date. Provided the equipment qualified as first-term SUE and continues to be used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED in the second period, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the ITC.

CCA Interaction and PDP Exclusions: The capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, it is depreciated under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8 (with any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reducing the Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year). SUE excludes used property, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)—defined as property that, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility, plant, or line, and intended over its expected useful life to use primarily for non-SR&ED purposes.

body.text: C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Incurred After December 15, 2024)

For lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 (reported on lines 350/355 and Part 6A Box 759 of Form T661), eligibility depends on the claimant's method election and percentage of operating time over the 12-month taxation year (or over the period after December 15, 2024 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024):

items: Under the Traditional Method: When leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, the claimant can claim 100% of the expenditure as a lease cost. When used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the proportional percentage of the lease cost used in SR&ED may be claimed on line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, provided it is directly attributable (directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Under the Proxy Method: Lease costs for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF)—desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators—are specifically excluded because they are covered by the 55% PPA. However, computers, computer hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are NOT GPOEF and qualify under the Proxy Method. For non-GPOEF equipment under the Proxy Method: (1) if used 90% or more (ASA) for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost can be claimed; (2) if used primarily (more than 50% up to less than 90%) for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost can be claimed (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and (3) if used 50% or less for SR&ED, no portion (0%) can be claimed.

Building Lease Exclusion: Under both methods, expenses incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (other than a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance) are strictly excluded.

body.text: 4.8 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and 20-Year ITC Recapture

Reduction for Assistance and Contract Payments (Subsections 127(18)–(22) and Paragraph 37(1)(d)): Both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool are reduced by any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance (amounts included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Assistance reduces expenditures on a project-by-project basis down to nil (any excess is included in income). Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance among themselves using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20). Repayments of assistance increase the Section 37 pool and generate a non-refundable ITC at the rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the pool.

20-Year ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)): Under subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a claimant must report ITC recapture (adding to Part I tax payable on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) when all four conditions are met:

items: The claimant acquired the property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36));

The cost of the property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure—specifically materials transformed, SR&ED capital property (pre-2014 or post-December 15, 2024), Shared-Use Equipment, or property acquired via an SR&ED contract (salaries, wages, overhead, and materials consumed are not subject to recapture);
A percentage of the cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and
The claimant disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use (or disposes of/converts another property incorporating the SR&ED property).

body.text: By CRA administrative policy (the de minimis rule), recapture rules will not be applied when: (1) proceeds from scrap sales of an experimental product are less than 10% of the property's total cost; (2) the fair market value (FMV) of an SR&ED output upon conversion or non-arm's length transfer is less than 10% of total cost; or (3) insurance proceeds for materials consumed are 10% or less of the cost of the materials. Furthermore, disposing of SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's length purchaser does not trigger recapture if the purchaser continues to use the property all or substantially all (≥90%) for SR&ED (subsections 127(33)–(34)).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer R&D tax incentives. Every provincial and territorial R&D tax credit (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer R&D tax credits) is treated as "government assistance" that reduces the federal Section 37 deductible pool and federal Section 127 qualified expenditures unless formally renounced/waived by the filing-due date.
5.1 Québec: The 2025 CRIC Overhaul and the IDCI Patent Box

Québec administers its corporate tax system independently through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec) (via corporate income tax return CO-17), while harmonizing its R&D definition with federal subsection 248(1) and relying on the CRA to conduct the scientific review of R&D work.
A. The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Codes 112 & 113)

Introduced in the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget Speech, the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation) applies to qualified corporations (or corporate members of qualified partnerships) for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.

Consolidation and Elimination of Seven Legacy Québec Tax Measures: To streamline innovation assistance, effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated seven prior tax measures (which remain claimable only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025): (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly Form RD-1029.7, where rates varied from 14% to 30%); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.16.1); (3) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.9.03); (4) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the Industrial Design Component of the Design Tax Credits (note: the fashion design component continues to be eligible); and (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts.
Universal Two-Tier Refundable Rate Structure (30% / 20%): The CRIC is 100% refundable for all qualified corporations regardless of their asset size, calculated at two tiers:

items: 30% Increased Rate: On the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, regardless of the corporation's assets (associated corporations carrying on a business in Québec allocate the $1,000,000 expenditure limit using Form RD-1029.8.EN); and
20% Basic Rate: On all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 maximum.

body.text: Expansion to Pre-Commercialization Activities and Capital Property: Alongside traditional R&D (reported under Code 112), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities (reported under Code 113) undertaken in Québec as a continuation of R&D carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities encompass: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements to obtain initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (2) product design (including form/aesthetics development, improved functionality, and material selection); and (3) quality control activities, strictly limited to implementing a quality control system required for initial approval or certification. Qualified expenditures for both R&D and pre-commercialization include: 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees in Québec; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for contracts carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of capital property acquisition costs in Québec (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and prohibiting double-dipping with the C3i tax credit for investment and innovation).
Modified Exclusion Threshold Formula: Qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of:

items: $50,000; or

The sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold, corresponding to the sum of the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax system for each employee (e.g., $18,571 in 2025, as illustrated in a third-party advisory analysis), adjusted according to the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

B. Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI / DICI — 2% Patent Box)

Québec also provides the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) (claimed on Form CO-737.18.CI), which allows a corporation with an establishment in Québec that commercializes a qualified intellectual property asset resulting from Québec R&D—specifically (1) an invention protected by a patent or certificate of supplementary protection, (2) software protected by copyright, or (3) a plant variety protected by a plant breeder's rights certificate—to benefit from an effective Québec corporate tax rate of 2% (a 9.5 percentage point reduction from the general 11.5% corporate rate) on qualified income derived from selling/leasing property incorporating the asset, supplying services intrinsically related to the asset, royalties, or judicial damages. For the purposes of calculating the Québec nexus ratio under the IDCI, R&D expenditures are not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, and pre-commercialization expenditures are not included in the nexus ratio calculation.
5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
The Province of Ontario offers three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA through the T2 corporate return.

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96 Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 566 / T2SCH566, Schedule 5 Line 468): An 8% fully refundable tax credit (10% prior to June 1, 2016) available to qualifying corporations on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per year (maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000). The $3,000,000 expenditure limit (shared among associated corporations) is gradually reduced if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Under the enacted rules, qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 40% of capital expenditures made before 2014, while capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 are excluded. To parallel Bill C-15, Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement (October 29, 2026) proposes to restore the eligibility of qualifying capital expenditures for the OITC for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024. A corporation can waive the OITC under subsection 96(14).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–44 Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 508 / T2SCH508, Schedule 5 Line 416): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (including 100% of current expenditures; restored eligibility of qualifying capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 is proposed in Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement), with no expenditure cap. Eligible expenditures for the ORDTC are reduced by the OITC (which is government assistance for ORDTC purposes). Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and carries forward 20 years, is subject to recapture on Schedule 508 (Schedule 5 line 277), and may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) so as not to reduce the federal SR&ED pool when a corporation cannot use non-refundable credits.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97 Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 568 & Schedule 569, Schedule 5 Line 470): A 20% fully refundable tax credit available to corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on qualified current expenditures made as a payment of money (not in-kind) under an eligible SR&ED contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—including Ontario universities, Ontario colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence operating in Ontario—provided the corporation is not connected to the ERI. Qualified expenditures are capped at $20,000,000 annually across associated corporations (maximum annual tax credit of $4,000,000), and a separate Schedule 569 with the ERI Code must be filed for each contract alongside Schedule 568.
