body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, Audit Administration, and Penalties
6.1 Statutory Filing Deadlines by Taxpayer Type

Under subsection 37(11) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. If the reporting deadline has passed, the CRA cannot accept missing prescribed information, and the SR&ED expenditures and related ITC are permanently lost:

items: Corporations (Form T2): The T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of the taxation year, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the tax year-end (except for a non-profit SR&ED corporation exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), whose reporting deadline is its T2 filing-due date, 6 months after tax year-end).

Individuals / Sole Proprietorships (Form T1): For an individual with a December 31 taxation year-end, the T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following year, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of June 15 of the second following year (17.5 months after year-end).

Trusts (Form T3): A trust's T3 filing-due date is no later than 90 days after the trust's tax year-end, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 15 months (90 days + 12 months) after the tax year-end (e.g., March 30, 2025 for a December 31, 2023 tax return).

Members of a Partnership: Individual or corporate partners must file Form T2038(IND) or Schedule T2SCH31 (along with a copy of the partnership's Form T661, partnership financial statements, and ITC allocation schedules) by their respective SR&ED reporting deadlines.

body.text: If Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the SR&ED reporting deadline, the claimant may still deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures in its Section 37 pool, but is not entitled to earn any ITC on those expenditures.
6.2 Anatomy of Form T661 (Parts 1 to 10) and Claim Preparer Penalties

To satisfy the prescribed information requirements of subsection 37(11), a claimant must complete Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) across all ten parts:

Part 1 (General Information) captures claimant identification and partnership details. Part 2 (Project Information: Sections A to C) captures technical project information for each project claimed, including project start and completion dates, Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome? — maximum 350 words), Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in Line 242?), Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve?), Section C supporting evidence checklists, and Line 262 (names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024). Under the Top 20 Projects Rule, claimants may choose to submit Part 2 with their return for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided the cost of every project claimed is included in Part 6 and completed Part 2 forms for all projects are maintained at the claimant's place of business for submission upon CRA request.

Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures: Sections A to C) captures the Traditional vs. Proxy method election (lines 160/162), allowable SR&ED expenditures, and the Section 37 deductible pool (lines 420–470). Part 4 (Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes) adds the PPA and SUE (line 504) and subtracts government/non-government assistance (lines 513–517), current expenditures unpaid after 180 days (line 520), non-taxable supplier contracts (line 528), the 20% reduction on arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (line 529), and prescribed expenditures (line 530). Part 5 (Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount) calculates the salary base and the 55% PPA on line 820. Part 6 (Project Costs) allocates project costs across all claimed projects, including Part 6A Box 759 (lease costs of equipment), Part 6B Box 782 (capital expenditure amount), and Part 6C Box 792 (25% of capital cost for SUE). Part 7 captures additional statistical information and Part 8 provides the claim checklist.

Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) and the $1,000 Penalty (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3) ITA): Part 9 requires prescribed information for each claim preparer that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, including billing arrangements. Under subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if the prescribed claim preparer information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (though missing or inaccurate Part 9 information does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself). Part 10 (Certification) requires the signature of an authorized signing officer.
6.3 CRA Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026), Review Process, and Dispute Resolution

New Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026): On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process through My Business Account. This process enables eligible businesses to find out whether their projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before they begin work or incur any costs, receiving a formal pre-claim approval determination from the CRA within eight weeks. When a filed claim includes pre-approved projects and requires only an expenditure review, the CRA processes the claim within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim (compared to the standard 180-calendar-day service standard for refundable claims selected for full review, and 60 calendar days for refundable claims processed without review). Potential claimants can also use the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), request a Pre-Claim Review (PCR), or participate in the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS); the free Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) service is no longer available as of January 1, 2026.

The Three-Step CRA Review Process and RTA Determinations: Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated in 2026), reviews are conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM):

items: Step 1 (The Start of the Review): The reviewer contacts the claimant by phone to identify the RTA and FR, confirm official language and secure communication preferences, outline the specific projects and issues selected for review, and send an initial letter with a meeting agenda and a 30-calendar-day timeline for pre-meeting information requests.

Step 2 (The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information): Conducted virtually or on-site, encompassing interviews with technical personnel who performed or supervised the work, a tour of the premises, examination of contemporaneous supporting evidence, and communication of preliminary findings.

Step 3 (The End of the Review): The RTA prepares an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report assigning one of five formal determinations—AW (All reviewed Work meets the definition of SR&ED), SW (Some reviewed Work meets the definition and some does not), NW (No claimed Work meets the definition), UN (Unsubstantiated), or AAF (Accepted As Filed without technical review)—and the FR computes financial adjustments. If adjustments or penalties are proposed, the claimant receives a proposal package and has 30 calendar days to submit written representations.

body.text: Three-Step Dispute Resolution and Notice of Objection (90 Days): Under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns, unresolved issues escalate through: (1) direct discussion with the RTA and/or FR; (2) discussion with the RTM and/or FRM; and (3) a formal Administrative Review by the Assistant Director (who determines whether due process was given and whether the reviews were consistent with legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in "Decision Maintained" or "Decision Reconsidered"). Following the issuance of a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, a claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection, and may subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
6.4 Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) ITA)

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a civil gross negligence penalty applies to every person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim (for example, claiming projects known not to involve SR&ED, claiming normal business expenses for activities that did not take place, or continuing to claim non-qualifying or unsubstantiated amounts after being advised in writing by the CRA). The CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. The penalty is calculated as the greater of:
Penalty = max($100, 50% × [Understated Part I Tax Payable + Refund of Overstated Refundable ITCs])

In computing this penalty, the CRA considers that overstated expenditures in the Section 37 pool and overstated ITCs are deducted first (calculating theoretical Part I tax understated where a net loss is reported by deeming taxable income not to be less than zero), and applies the 50% penalty to the entire overstated refund of refundable ITCs.
6.5 Interaction Between NRC IRAP Grants and SR&ED Tax Credits

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides technical advisory services (through Industrial Technology Advisors, ITAs) and non-repayable financial assistance to incorporated, for-profit Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees, including core R&D funding and the Youth Employment Program (supporting placements of 6 to 12 months for post-secondary graduates aged 15 to 30).

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), NRC IRAP financial assistance is government assistance (reported on Form T661 line 515) that reduces the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures. However, because NRC IRAP cost-shares only direct salary costs (leaving the business responsible for benefits and overhead), an NRC IRAP salary grant does not reduce the claimant's eligible salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 when computing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). For example, if an SME incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salary and receives an $80,000 NRC IRAP salary grant, its pre-assistance qualified expenditures under the Proxy Method are $100,000 (salary) + $55,000 (55% PPA on the full $100,000 salary) = $155,000; subtracting the $80,000 IRAP assistance leaves $75,000 in net qualified SR&ED expenditures, which at the 35% enhanced ITC rate generates $26,250 in federal SR&ED cash refund in addition to the $80,000 IRAP grant.
7. Judicial Precedents, Case Law Evolution, and Documentation Standards
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. (1998)

The foundational judicial authority governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is the decision of Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). Interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED, Justice Bowman articulated the five-question approach that governs Canadian tax courts:

items: Is there a technical risk or uncertainty which cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty (though system uncertainty—arising from integrating known components into a complex system—can qualify).

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This entails a five-stage methodology: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advance, that is, an advancement in the general understanding of technology?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 7.2 Federal Court of Appeal Endorsements and Refinements (1998–2022)
The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) has consistently upheld Justice Bowman's five criteria in Northwest Hydraulic as the binding interpretation of subsection 248(1):

items: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, (1998) 99 D.T.C. 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA): At paragraph 10, the FCA endorsed the approach in Northwest Hydraulic and emphasized the necessity of documentary evidence of repeatable testing and recorded data.

C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393: Writing for a unanimous court (Stone, Evans, and Sexton JJ.A., at para. 17), Justice Sexton confirmed that the five criteria in Northwest Hydraulic are useful in determining whether an activity is SR&ED and were approved by the FCA in RIS-Christie.

Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355: At paragraph 6, the FCA confirmed that the criteria for determining whether work qualifies as SR&ED are those set out in Northwest Hydraulic, underscoring that the SR&ED program is intended to subsidize overcoming technological uncertainty to achieve technological advancement and was never intended to subsidize routine product development.
R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152: At paragraph 4, the FCA again endorsed the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.

Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 88 (Docket A-442-19, May 10, 2021): The appellant argued that because the text of subsection 248(1) contains no explicit reference to the "scientific method," the Tax Court judge (Owen J.) erred in applying the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion. Writing for the FCA (concurred in by Near and Mactavish JJ.A.), Justice Webb dismissed the appeal, holding (at paras. 6–8) that in setting out the five criteria in Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman was interpreting the definition of SR&ED as endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation.

National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 70, aff'd 2022 FCA (Docket A-231-20): As summarized in legal commentary, the FCA dismissed the consulting firm's appeal and affirmed the Tax Court decision, ruling that the appellant's challenge to the Northwest Hydraulic criteria had already been settled in Kam-Press Metal.

body.text: 7.3 Recent Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence (2017–2025): Trial-and-Error vs. Systematic Investigation

Recent Tax Court of Canada rulings between 2017 and late 2025 (as reported in court records and legal practitioner analyses) highlight the decisive boundary between routine trial-and-error and systematic investigation:

Appeal Allowed (Taxpayer won $343,449 in QREs and $60,963 in ITCs for 2013/2015/2016 plus 2014 claims)

As noted in legal commentary, the taxpayer succeeded because it produced compelling, contemporaneous records of technological uncertainties, hypothesis formulation, hypothesis modification, testing, and results.

As noted in tax law commentary citing para. 119 of the decision, while contemporaneous technical records are vital, contemporaneous time sheets are not necessarily required for work to qualify as eligible SR&ED.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159
Food & beverage chemistry (room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based drink)

As analysed in tax advisory commentary: (1) technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution (Chiber) exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context; (2) contemporaneous records need not be designed for an outsider unfamiliar with the field to replicate results; (3) the five Northwest Hydraulic questions remain a valid methodology alongside CRA's "how and why" approach.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC (May 2, 2025) & Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC (Oct 14, 2025)
Practitioner analysis confirms that credible oral testimony at trial cannot substitute for contemporaneous records created during the work showing iterative hypothesis testing.
Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC (Sept 25, 2025)
Civil/materials engineering (mobile concrete placement & hydration chemistry)

Practitioner commentary highlights Justice Sorensen's "Photographer Test": reactively adjusting known parameters (like a skilled photographer adjusting aperture, shutter speed, and ISO) with only basic journal entries constitutes trial-and-error / routine engineering, not systematic investigation.

body.text: 8. Comprehensive Worked Mathematical Examples
8.1 Worked Example 1: CCPC Enhanced 35% ITC, Taxable Capital Phase-Out, and Ontario OITC/ORDTC Stacking (2026 Taxation Year)

Scenario: InnovateTech Inc. is a qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) operating solely through a permanent establishment in Toronto, Ontario, with a taxation year running from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (post-December 15, 2024 rules under Bill C-15 apply). Its prior-year (2025) federal taxable income was $350,000 (below the $500,000 Ontario OITC taxable income threshold and below its federal qualifying income limit of $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − $15,000,000) ÷ $60,000,000] = $375,000) and its prior-year (2025) taxable capital employed in Canada was $30,000,000. In 2026, InnovateTech elects the Proxy Method and incurs the following eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (all non-specified employees): $3,000,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries and wages; $400,000 in materials consumed in SR&ED; $500,000 in arm's-length Ontario SR&ED subcontractor payments (to taxable suppliers); and $600,000 for new SR&ED laboratory equipment acquired on March 1, 2026 and used 95% (ASA ≥90%) for SR&ED in Canada.
Step 1 — Calculate Pre-Assistance Federal Allowable and Qualified SR&ED Expenditures:

items: Section 37 Deductible Pool Additions (Pre-Assistance): $3,000,000 (Wages) + $400,000 (Materials) + $500,000 (Contracts at 100%) + $600,000 (Capital at 100%) = $4,500,000.
Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA — Regulation 2900(4)): 55% × $3,000,000 (Salary Base) = $1,650,000.

Pre-Assistance Section 127 Qualified Expenditures (QREs): $3,000,000 (Wages) + $1,650,000 (PPA) + $400,000 (Materials) + $400,000 (Arm's-Length Contracts at 80% × $500,000) + $600,000 (New ASA Capital Equipment at 100%) = $6,050,000 (comprising $5,450,000 in current QREs/PPA and $600,000 in capital QREs).

body.text: Step 2 — Calculate Ontario Provincial Tax Credits (OITC and ORDTC):

items: Ontario OITC (8% Refundable — Schedule 566): Because prior-year taxable capital ($30,000,000) is between Ontario's $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 phase-out thresholds, InnovateTech's $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is reduced linearly: OITC Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × ( ($50,000,000 − $30,000,000) ÷ ($50,000,000 − $25,000,000) ) = $2,400,000 Since total QREs ($6,050,000) exceed the $2,400,000 OITC limit, the OITC earned is 8% × $2,400,000 = $192,000 (100% refundable).

Ontario ORDTC (3.5% Non-Refundable — Schedule 508): Assuming enactment of the capital-expenditure restoration proposed in Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement, the ORDTC base is total Ontario QREs ($6,050,000) reduced by the OITC ($192,000), which equals $5,858,000; multiplying by 3.5% yields $205,030 in ORDTC. Total Ontario government assistance is $192,000 + $205,030 = $397,030 (allocating the OITC to current expenditures first, $600,000 × 3.5% = $21,000 of ORDTC reduces capital QREs to $579,000, and the remaining $376,030 of Ontario credits reduces current QREs from $5,450,000 to $5,073,970; total net federal QREs = $6,050,000 − $397,030 = $5,652,970).

body.text: Step 3 — Calculate Federal Expenditure Limit and Federal SR&ED ITC:

items: Under the enacted Bill C-15 rules ($15M–$75M phase-out on a $6M limit), $30,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital reduces the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit as follows: Federal Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ( ($60,000,000 − ($30,000,000 − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000 ) = $4,500,000
Enhanced 35% ITC on the first $4,500,000 of net QREs (applied to current QREs/PPA): 35% × $4,500,000 = $1,575,000 (100% refundable).

Basic 15% ITC on the remaining $1,152,970 of net QREs above the $4,500,000 expenditure limit ($573,970 remaining current QREs + $579,000 net capital QREs): 15% × $1,152,970 = $172,945.50 (40% refundable for a Qualifying CCPC = $69,178.20 cash refund, with the remaining $103,767.30 available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 / forward 20 years).
Total Combined Federal + Ontario Credits: $1,575,000 + $172,945.50 + $192,000 + $205,030 = $2,144,975.50.

body.text: 8.2 Worked Example 2: Specified Employee Salary Caps and PPA Calculation (2026 YMPE = $74,600)

Scenario: FounderCo Inc. (a CCPC with a December 31, 2026 taxation year-end, where 2026 YMPE = $74,600) employs its sole shareholder, Dr. Jane Doe (a specified employee for all 365 days of 2026), and one non-shareholder software architect, Alex Smith (a non-specified employee). In 2026, Dr. Jane Doe is paid $420,000 base salary plus a $50,000 year-end bonus and spends 80% of her time directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED in Canada. Alex Smith is paid $150,000 base salary plus a $20,000 performance bonus (paid within 60 days of year-end) plus $5,000 in cash taxable benefits under section 6, and spends 92% (ASA ≥90%) of his time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada.
Step 1 — Allowable SR&ED Salaries and Wages (Part 3 of Form T661):

items: Dr. Jane Doe (Line 305 — Specified Employee): Her $50,000 bonus is disallowed under paragraph 37(9)(a). Her raw SR&ED salary share is 80% × $420,000 = $336,000. Because $336,000 is below the 2026 subsection 37(9.1) cap of 5 × $74,600 = $373,000, the full $336,000 is allowable on line 305.

Alex Smith (Line 300 — Non-Specified Employee): Because Alex spent ≥90% (ASA) of his time directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of his eligible remuneration (including bonuses and cash taxable benefits for a non-specified employee) is allowable: $150,000 + $20,000 + $5,000 = $175,000 on line 300.
Total Allowable SR&ED Wages: $336,000 + $175,000 = $511,000.

body.text: Step 2 — Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base (Part 5 of Form T661):

items: Alex Smith (Non-Specified Employee PPA Base): Under Regulation 2900(9), his $20,000 bonus and $5,000 section 6 taxable benefit are excluded from the salary base, leaving 100% (under the ≥90% ASA rule in Regulation 2900(5)) of his base salary: $150,000.

Dr. Jane Doe (Specified Employee PPA Base — Lines 852–858): Under Regulation 2900(7), her salary base inclusion is the lesser of: (1) 80% directly engaged share of base salary ($336,000 on line 856); (2) 75% of total base salary (75% × $420,000 = $315,000 under paragraph 2900(7)(a)); and (3) 2.5 × YMPE (2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500 on line 858 under paragraph 2900(7)(b)). Thus, her PPA salary base inclusion is capped at $186,500.
Total PPA Salary Base and 55% PPA (Line 820): Total salary base = $150,000 + $186,500 = $336,500; multiplying by 55% yields a PPA of $185,075.00.

body.text: 8.3 Worked Example 3: Québec CRIC (30% / 20%) and Federal SR&ED Stacking (Taxation Year Beginning After March 25, 2025)

Scenario: Montréal AI Labs Inc. is a CCPC operating in Montréal, Québec, with a taxation year running from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (subject to the new Québec CRIC regime and federal Bill C-15 rules). It employs 10 full-time (100%) R&D software engineers in Québec at $120,000 salary each ($1,200,000 total R&D wages), employs 2 full-time (100%) pre-commercialization engineers in Québec conducting regulatory certification testing and product design at $100,000 salary each ($200,000 total pre-commercialization wages), and acquires $300,000 in new dedicated R&D server hardware in Québec (used 100% ASA for R&D).
Step 1 — Calculate Québec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR):

items: Gross Québec CRIC Expenditures: $1,200,000 (R&D Wages, Code 112) + $300,000 (R&D Capital Equipment, Code 112) + $200,000 (Pre-Commercialization Wages, Code 113) = $1,700,000.

Exclusion Threshold: Greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec Basic Personal Amount per employee prorated by R&D / pre-commercialization time. Using the illustrative basic personal amount of $18,571 per full-time employee from third-party advisory analysis across 12 full-time employees (10 R&D + 2 pre-commercialization) gives 12 × $18,571 = $222,852 ($185,710 attributable to R&D and $37,142 to Pre-Commercialization).
Net CRIC Expenditure Base: $1,700,000 − $222,852 = $1,477,148.
Two-Tier CRIC Calculation:
Tier 1 (First $1,000,000 at 30%): $1,000,000 × 30% = $300,000.00.
Tier 2 (Remaining $477,148 at 20%): $477,148 × 20% = $95,429.60.
Total Refundable Québec CRIC: $300,000.00 + $95,429.60 = $395,429.60.

body.text: Step 2 — Calculate Federal SR&ED ITC (Form T661 & Schedule T2SCH31):

items: Pre-Assistance Federal QREs (covering the 10 R&D engineers and $300,000 R&D capital equipment; pre-commercialization product design and regulatory certification are excluded from federal SR&ED under paragraphs 248(1)(f)/(i)/(j)): $1,200,000 (R&D Wages) + $660,000 (55% PPA on $1,200,000) + $300,000 (R&D Capital Equipment) = $2,160,000.

Subtract Québec CRIC Attributable to Federal R&D Activities: Net Québec R&D expenditures ($1,500,000 − $185,710 = $1,314,290) represent 88.9748% of total net CRIC expenditures ($1,477,148), so 88.9748% × $395,429.60 = $351,832.84 of the CRIC is government assistance in respect of federal SR&ED. Subtracting $351,832.84 from $2,160,000 leaves a Net Federal QRE Pool of $1,808,167.16.
Federal Enhanced 35% ITC: 35% × $1,808,167.16 = $632,858.51.
Total Combined Federal SR&ED + Québec CRIC Refund: $632,858.51 + $395,429.60 = $1,028,288.11 on $1,700,000 of total innovation outlays (an effective 60.49% recovery).

body.text: 9. Audit Readiness and Compliance Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To ensure full compliance with the Income Tax Act, the Income Tax Regulations, and Tax Court of Canada evidentiary standards, Canadian SR&ED and provincial R&D claimants should execute the following five-point verification protocol during each taxation year:

items: Upfront Pre-Claim Approval Assessment: For new or high-value R&D projects, evaluate submitting an optional Pre-Claim Approval application through CRA My Business Account before beginning work or incurring costs to obtain an upfront technical eligibility determination within eight weeks and qualify for the 90-calendar-day expenditure review standard.

Contemporaneous Technical Record-Keeping (Northwest Hydraulic Question 5): Generate and retain dated, versioned records as the work progresses—including formulated hypotheses, structured experimental test protocols, quantitative test measurements (avoiding the naked-eye observation failure in Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6), failed trial logs, source code commit histories, and analytical conclusions—clearly separating systematic investigation from reactive trial-and-error (Paveit Construction, 2025 TCC).

Time-Tracking and Specified Employee Compensation Structuring: Maintain project time sheets or task-allocation logs (noting that while DAZZM Inc., 2024 TCC 129 observed that time sheets are not an absolute statutory prerequisite, they remain primary audit evidence). Pay founder/specified employee remuneration as regular T4 salary rather than dividends or bonuses (which are excluded under paragraph 37(9)(a)), and ensure all accrued wages and current expenditures are paid within 180 days of taxation year-end under subsections 78(4) and 127(26).

Capital Property, SUE, and Lease Operating-Time Logs (Post-December 15, 2024): Maintain operating-time logs over the full taxation year for all depreciable equipment and leased assets acquired after December 15, 2024 to substantiate either the 90% ASA threshold (for 100% capital expenditure or lease claims) or the >50% to <90% primarily threshold (for 25%/25% first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment or 50% Proxy Method lease claims).

Prescribed Forms, Claim Preparer Disclosures, and Statutory Deadlines: File Form T661 (completing Part 9 claim preparer disclosures accurately to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)), Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND), non-arm's length agreements (Forms T1145, T1146, T1174, T1263, and Schedule T2SCH49), and provincial schedules (Québec Forms RD-1029.8.CR and RD-222, Ontario Schedules 566/508/568/569, B.C. Form T666, Alberta AT1 Schedule 29, or Saskatchewan/Manitoba/Atlantic/Yukon schedules) strictly on or before the 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline (18 months after corporate tax year-end). Where a corporation in Ontario, B.C., Saskatchewan, or Manitoba is in a tax loss position, evaluate formally waiving or renouncing non-refundable provincial R&D credits by the T2 filing-due date so they do not erode the federal 35% refundable SR&ED pool.
